passage: The design studio's Friday review ran late. Shalini, an intern, pinned her poster to the board and waited. Nitin, her boyfriend and a junior designer there, stood near the front. When Hema's layout went up, he leaned in. "Look at that spacing. She makes it look effortless," he said, loud enough for everyone. People nodded. Shalini's own poster suddenly looked crowded to her, the colours too loud. She tugged her sleeves over her hands and stared at her shoes. At lunch she barely touched her rice. "You okay?" Nitin asked. "Fine," she said, then scrolled through Hema's portfolio under the table, counting every award, and each one felt like a mark against her own name.

qa.q: Whose layout did Nitin praise at the Friday review?
qa.a: Nitin praised Hema's layout, saying she makes it look effortless.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when she looked back at her own poster?
qa.a: She felt smaller and less talented; her poster suddenly seemed crowded and too loud to her after Nitin's praise of Hema.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Shalini at this early stage?
qa.a: She could notice that she is ranking herself against Hema and name that to herself, or tell Nitin honestly that the comment stung, before the comparison hardens into suspicion.

qa.q: How might Nitin see lunch from his side?
qa.a: He probably thinks he just admired good work and is puzzled why Shalini says "fine" but hardly eats.

grounding: It shows a young woman who hears her partner praise a colleague's skill and quietly measures herself against that colleague.

passage:
Dear Ruchi,
You asked why I sounded flat on the phone. Here it is. Omkar took me to his office dinner on Saturday. His teammate Revati played the guitar after dessert, and she was honestly brilliant. Omkar clapped the loudest and said, "She can do anything, that one." I smiled and clapped too. Then the whole way home I kept thinking: I cannot sing, I cannot play, I am just the girl who organises things. His friend Tushar asked what I do and I mumbled "accounts" like it was a confession. Omkar did nothing wrong, I know that. But I lay awake measuring my small list against her long one, and my list kept losing.
Miss you. Call me Sunday?
Ketaki

qa.q: What did Revati do after dessert at the office dinner?
qa.a: Revati played the guitar after dessert.

qa.q: How can you tell Ketaki felt inferior after the dinner?
qa.a: She felt small and not good enough: she lay awake comparing her talents to Revati's and even said "accounts" to Tushar like it was a confession.

qa.q: What would you advise Ketaki at this point?
qa.a: To notice that her hurt comes from comparing herself, not from anything Omkar did, and to write down what she values in herself, maybe sharing the feeling with Omkar gently. 🙂

qa.q: How might Omkar remember the same evening?
qa.a: He likely remembers a fun dinner where a teammate played well, with no idea that his praise left Ketaki feeling she had nothing to offer.

grounding: It illustrates a young woman who feels lesser after her partner admires a colleague's talent, with jealousy rooted in comparison.

passage:
Counselling note, college wellness centre.
Indu, second-year student, came in for her follow-up. She opened her phone before sitting down and showed me three things: Vaibhav had taken four hours to reply to her message, he had liked a classmate's beach photo, and he had gone to a friend's birthday dinner without inviting her. "Put it together," she said. Her voice was quick and her knee kept bouncing. I asked what else had happened this week. After a pause she said he had brought her tea during exams, called every night and introduced her to his cousins. She looked surprised hearing herself. I noted that she had not counted any of those.
Next step: I suggested she write both lists before our next session and bring them.

qa.q: How long did Vaibhav take to reply to Indu's message?
qa.a: Vaibhav had taken four hours to reply.

qa.q: What does Indu's surprise suggest when she lists the good things?
qa.a: It suggests she had stopped noticing those facts; her fear was making her collect only the things that seemed to prove it.

qa.q: What turning point does the counsellor offer at this stage?
qa.a: Writing both lists helps Indu see that her mind is filtering for evidence, which gives her a chance to question the story before she acts on it.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav be experiencing right now?
qa.a: He may feel that ordinary things like a late reply or a like are being treated as crimes, and he may be confused about what he did wrong.

grounding: It shows a young woman turning a late reply, a like and a night out into proof while overlooking the ordinary facts against her fear.

passage:
Tuesday, 11:40 pm
Kishore said he'd be home from football by nine. It's nearly midnight. He posted a photo from the café after, and that girl from his team is in the corner of it, laughing. He liked her comment too. I've zoomed in on that photo maybe ten times. 😔
He did text "running late, love you" at 9:15. I know. And he left his match early last week just to fetch me from the station. And he told me about the café plan yesterday.
Why does my brain skip all that and go straight to her face in the corner? It's like I'm a girl detective who only collects clues for one answer.
Not sending anything tonight. Sleeping on it.
— Gurleen

qa.q: What did Kishore text at 9:15?
qa.a: He texted "running late, love you" at 9:15.

qa.q: Why does Gurleen keep zooming in on the photo?
qa.a: She is afraid Kishore likes the girl from his team, so her mind is searching for proof and treating a laughing face as a clue.

qa.q: What small step at this stage could stop the spiral from growing?
qa.a: Choosing to sleep on it instead of sending an accusing message is a good step; tomorrow she could look at all the facts, including his text and the station pickup.

qa.q: How would Kishore probably feel if Gurleen confronted him about the photo?
qa.a: He would likely feel confused and hurt, since he told her the plan, texted when late and has been showing care.

grounding: It illustrates how a slow return, a like and a group photo become evidence in a suspicious mind that skips the reassuring facts.

passage: Snow was piling against the window of the Toronto flat when Tariq came back from his shift. "Oh, you're home," Amira said. "Thought you might stay out with your new favourite coworker." She laughed, but it came out thin. Tariq frowned and put the groceries down. Later she took her plate to the bedroom and shut the door, waiting to see if he would knock. He did, after twenty minutes, looking tired. While he showered, his phone lit up on the bed. Her hand hovered. She picked it up, read nothing but a delivery message, and felt no better at all. When he came out, he saw the phone in a different spot. He said nothing, and the silence sat between them all evening.

qa.q: Where did Tariq's phone light up?
qa.a: His phone lit up on the bed while he showered.

qa.q: Why did Amira shut the bedroom door with her plate?
qa.a: She wanted to test whether Tariq would come after her, hoping it would prove he still cared.

qa.q: What turning point is available for Amira now?
qa.a: Instead of more tests, she could tell Tariq plainly that she has been feeling insecure, because the checks are not calming her and are starting to hurt him.

qa.q: How is Tariq likely experiencing these tests?
qa.a: He seems worn out and uneasy; the joke, the closed door and the moved phone may make him feel watched and distrusted. 😔

grounding: It shows a young woman using half-joking jabs, withdrawal to see if he follows, and a phone check that brings no reassurance and strains both people.

passage: The hostel common room was empty except for Himani and Parth, sharing a packet of chips before the library closed. "So, is your lab partner coming to the fest too?" she asked, grinning a little too wide. "Maybe you two can present together, you're such a team." Parth laughed awkwardly. "Himani, she's just my lab partner." "Relax, I'm joking." Her friend Pallavi, passing with a laundry bucket, caught Himani's eye and raised an eyebrow. Later Himani didn't answer Parth's goodnight text, just to see if he'd call. He called twice, then stopped. Next morning he looked like he hadn't slept. "Are we okay?" he asked, and she heard herself say, "You tell me."

qa.q: Where were Himani and Parth sharing chips?
qa.a: They were in the hostel common room.

qa.q: What might Himani want when she ignores Parth's goodnight text?
qa.a: She seems to want proof that he cares enough to chase her, because she is afraid of losing him to his lab partner.

qa.q: What could turn things around for Himani at this stage?
qa.a: She could drop the half jokes and the silence and tell Parth honestly that she feels insecure, so he is not left guessing.

qa.q: What is it like for Parth right now?
qa.a: He looks sleepless and unsure, asking "Are we okay?" because the jokes and silence leave him worried without knowing why.

grounding: It illustrates provoking with teasing remarks and pulling away to test the partner, which wears both of them down.

passage:
"Who was that?" Lavanya asked as Sarvesh put his phone face down.
"My cousin. About Sunday lunch."
"You turned it over."
"Because last time you read my messages, Lavanya. I just want one thing that's mine."
"If there's nothing to hide, why do you need a thing that's yours?"
Sarvesh rubbed his eyes. "I haven't done anything. For months I've explained every late reply, every photo. I'm tired of being on trial."
"And I'm tired of you hiding."
"I'm not hiding! I'm protecting myself."
Lavanya's mother called from the kitchen, "Dinner's getting cold, you two."
Neither moved. Sarvesh took his phone to the balcony. Lavanya watched the closed glass door and felt her fears grow louder with every minute he stayed out there.

qa.q: Who did Sarvesh say had messaged him?
qa.a: He said it was his cousin, about Sunday lunch.

qa.q: How does Sarvesh feel about being questioned again?
qa.a: He feels distrusted without reason and exhausted, saying he is tired of being on trial.

qa.q: What turning point could break this loop?
qa.a: One of them could pause and name the pattern out loud, for example that his privacy feels like hiding to her and her questions feel like accusation to him, instead of defending their own side.

qa.q: How does Lavanya read Sarvesh going to the balcony?
qa.a: She takes it as more proof he is hiding something, which makes her fears grow while he only wanted space.

grounding: It shows a partner who feels distrusted and keeps more privacy, which the other reads as hiding, so each one's protection confirms the other's fear.

passage:
I'm Imran, and this is about last winter with Rehana.
At first I didn't mind her questions. Where were you, who was that. I answered, even showed my phone once. But it never ended. One night she asked why I'd smiled at a text, and something in me went cold. I thought: I have done nothing, and I'm still guilty.
So I started keeping things to myself. I changed my phone lock. I went for long walks alone. It felt like breathing room. To Rehana it looked exactly like a man with a secret.
The more she pushed, the more I closed; the more I closed, the more she pushed. Looking back, we were both scared, and we were both making it worse.

qa.q: What did Imran change on his phone?
qa.a: He changed his phone lock.

qa.q: What did Imran feel the night Rehana asked why he smiled at a text?
qa.a: He felt something go cold, a mix of hurt and resentment at being treated as guilty when he had done nothing.

qa.q: What could Imran have tried instead of quietly closing off?
qa.a: He could have told Rehana calmly that her checking made him feel distrusted and that his walks were for breathing room, so his privacy did not look like a secret.

qa.q: How did Rehana likely see Imran's long walks alone?
qa.a: She probably saw them as proof that he was hiding something, which pushed her to question him even more.

grounding: It illustrates the partner's side of the spiral, where feeling wrongly distrusted leads him to guard his privacy and that guarding feeds her suspicion.

subtype: Stage 5: Owning the feeling without accusing [Response]
passage:
Sit, Pranav, let me tell you something since you asked about fights with your girlfriend. When I was twenty-one, before I married your uncle Mohan, I was very jealous. Every time he mentioned a woman from his office, I would go quiet or ask twenty questions. One evening, after a week of this, I sat him down on the steps of the old library. My hands were cold. I said, "When you talk about her, I feel insecure. That is my feeling, and I have to work on it. I would like you to reassure me, but I will not ask you to prove anything." He took my hand and said he was glad I told him. That was the first calm talk we ever had. So, beta, say what you feel, not what the other did.
— your Vidya aunty

qa.q: Where did Vidya aunty sit Mohan down to talk?
qa.a: She sat him down on the steps of the old library.

qa.q: What do Vidya aunty's cold hands suggest about that evening?
qa.a: They suggest she was nervous and vulnerable, because owning her insecurity felt risky.

qa.q: Why did this talk become a turning point in the story?
qa.a: Vidya aunty named her feeling and took responsibility for it without accusing Mohan or demanding proof, which let him respond with care instead of defending himself.

qa.q: How did Mohan experience that talk?
qa.a: He felt trusted rather than accused, so he could take her hand and say he was glad she told him.

grounding: It shows a young woman sharing her insecurity as her own to work on, asking for reassurance without demanding proof, which invites care.

subtype: Stage 5: Owning the feeling without accusing [Response]
passage: The bus depot was roaring with engines and Vidya had only a few minutes before her bus to Pune left. She called Raghav, pressing one finger to her other ear. The line kept breaking. "Raghav? Can you hear me? I want to say something before I lose you." She took a breath. "When you go out with your college group and I hear nothing, I feel insecure. I know that's mine to handle, not yours. I'd love a little reassurance sometimes. I'm not asking you to send photos or prove anything." The line crackled. Then his voice came back, soft. "Thank you for telling me like that. I'll message you when I get there, okay?" The conductor whistled. Vidya climbed on, lighter.

qa.q: Where was Vidya going when she called Raghav?
qa.a: Her bus was going to Pune.

qa.q: How can you tell Vidya felt relieved after the call?
qa.a: She climbed on the bus feeling lighter, after Raghav answered her softly and warmly. 😊

qa.q: What made Vidya's way of speaking work even on a bad line?
qa.a: She spoke about her own feeling, said it was hers to handle and asked for reassurance without demanding photos or proof, so Raghav did not have to defend himself.

qa.q: What would change if Vidya had accused Raghav instead?
qa.a: He might have argued or gone quiet, and the noisy, broken call would likely have ended in a fight instead of an offer to message her.

grounding: It illustrates owning insecurity without blame and asking for reassurance rather than proof, which draws a caring reply even under time pressure.

passage:
Sunday night
Third pottery class today. My bowl collapsed twice and I laughed so hard with Tsering that the teacher had to shush us. 🙂 Didn't check my phone for two whole hours. That's new. Mum says I'm a calmer girl these days.
Sahil picked me up after and told me about his day without me asking, including lunch with his team. Old me would have asked who sat where. Today I just listened. It helps that he's the same every day, calls when he says he'll call.
I still get the tight chest sometimes. Thursday is my second session with the campus counsellor. She says the feeling can shrink when my life has more in it than him.
I think she's right. My bowl is drying on the windowsill.
— Dolma

subtype: Stage 1: The juicy piece of news [Actor]
passage:
Dear Diary,
Today at break I went to the office to give Ma'am my permission slip. Swati from my class was sitting on the bench outside, crying into her dupatta. Then I heard the office lady say on the phone, "...her father, the hospital, the whole family is..." and then she shut the door.
I walked back to class so fast. My heart was going thump thump. Nobody else knows! Not even Meenu, and Meenu knows everything. I felt like the most important girl in class 4. I kept thinking of how everyone would look at me if I told them.
I feel a bit bad for Swati. She looked really sad. But I also want to tell someone SO much.
Neelam

qa.q: Where was Swati sitting when Neelam saw her?
qa.a: Swati was sitting on the bench outside the office, crying into her dupatta.

qa.q: Why is Neelam so excited about what she heard?
qa.a: She knows something no one else does, not even Meenu, and she likes imagining how everyone would look at her if she told.

qa.q: What could Neelam do at this moment instead of passing it on?
qa.a: She could keep the half-heard words to herself, since she did not hear the whole story, and maybe just be kind to Swati tomorrow.

qa.q: How might Swati feel if the story spreads around class?
qa.a: She would likely feel hurt and embarrassed, because her family trouble is private and she is already upset. 😢

grounding: It shows a child who sees a crying classmate and overhears a fragment about her family, feeling important and eager to share it.

passage: The school in Rampura had only four classrooms and one tin-roofed office. At lunch Preeti went to fill her bottle at the hand pump near the office and saw Jyoti on the step, wiping her eyes with both wrists. Inside, the headmaster was talking to Jyoti's uncle. Preeti caught only "...land... her father... in the city now..." before Jagdish-ji the peon shooed her away. She ran back to the neem tree where the girls were eating. Her cheeks were hot. Words bubbled in her mouth like a boiling pot. She sat down, opened her tiffin, and leaned toward the others. "Guess what I just heard," she began, feeling taller than she had all week.

passage: On the auto ride home from school in Kochi, Seema pressed close to her best friend Jomon. "Promise you won't tell?" Jomon nodded hard. "Lekha's aunty came to school, crying. I think her parents are fighting. Maybe they're even going to separate." Seema had only seen the aunty's red eyes. The fighting part just slipped out, and it made the story sound bigger. Jomon's mouth fell open. "Really?" "Really," Seema said, and somehow, saying it the second time, it sounded like something she had seen herself. At home, while she ate her banana chips, she told her little brother the same thing, with the word "separate" said even more surely.

qa.q: What did Seema actually see at school?
qa.a: She had only seen the aunty's red eyes.

qa.q: How can you tell Seema was starting to believe her own guess?
qa.a: Saying it a second time made it sound like something she had seen herself, and she repeated "separate" even more surely to her brother.

qa.q: What could Seema do to stop the story growing?
qa.a: She could tell Jomon that she only saw red eyes and guessed the rest, and stop repeating it.

qa.q: How might Jomon see the story now?
qa.a: Jomon probably believes it is true because Seema said "really" so confidently, and may pass it on as fact.

grounding: It shows a child retelling news to her best friend, adding a guessed detail that sounds truer each time it is told.

passage:
"Arnab, come here, I have to tell you something," Gopika whispered, pulling him behind the living room curtain.
"What?"

passage: In the school library, Chandrika pretended to read but watched the corner table. Four girls had their heads together. "Don't tell anyone, okay?" one whispered, and the story moved from ear to ear like a passed note. Amandeep sat at the edge, not part of the group usually. She leaned in, listened, then added, "I heard that too," though Chandrika was sure she hadn't. The girls turned to her, smiling, and made space on the bench. Amandeep's shoulders relaxed. When the librarian came past, they all went silent and opened their books. Chandrika looked at the table of whispering heads and wondered who in there actually knew anything, and who just wanted to belong.

passage: When Pooja got off the tempo at the village school gate, two girls near the well looked at her and giggled. In class, someone passed a note behind her. qa.a: She could tell her teacher or her mother what is being said, so an adult can help stop the story instead of her facing it alone.

qa.a: He may feel awkward and unsure whether he did right, but perhaps also that she deserved to know.

grounding: It shows a girl noticing stares and giggles, learning a partly false story about her family, and feeling shame, anger and confusion.

passage: The bell rang at Dalia's school in Accra, and as she walked to her locker, two boys stopped talking and grinned. A girl near the stairs covered her mouth.
